title: Own the Thermometer — $100 sensors as prediction-market edge
thesis: A student cleared $100K+ on Polymarket weather contracts with a dorm-built weather station. The catalog also holds the rest of that kit, but in other collections: a cheap dish plus SDR that pulls live weather-satellite images, NASA's free event feed, and the websocket and order tooling the Polymarket automators use. Put first-party physical sensing in front of an automated limit-order bot and you get an edge that better math can't copy, because the input data is yours alone.
why_it_matters: Prediction markets now list contracts on physical outcomes like temperature, rainfall, wildfires and grid events. These contracts settle on a slow official reading. Whoever measures the same thing sooner and closer gets minutes of lead time, and that lead time is the whole trade.
novelty: The quant entries chase alpha in models like Kalman filters, the Ising model and Hawkes processes, while the hardware entries never mention markets. Only one creator in 846 entries crosses the line, and the catalog's own takeaway says it plainly: 'real edge = exclusive real-time data source, not better ML'.

action_sketch: Pick ONE contract family whose resolution source you can physically sit near (e.g. daily high temp at a named airport ASOS station). Read the exact settlement rule before buying hardware.
Put up a calibrated station (Ecowitt/Davis + Raspberry Pi logger) plus NOAA METAR polling, and log your reading vs the official one minute-by-minute for 30 days. Paper-trade only.
Wire a Polymarket websocket listener + limit-order bot (from the Polymarket/Kalshi repo) that fires only when your sensor and the order book disagree past a threshold; size tiny.

Falsifier: if your sensor's lead over the official reading is under the time it takes the book to reprice (check the websocket timestamps), or the error between your sensor and the station is wider than the contract buckets, there is no edge — stop.
prerequisites: Jurisdiction where Polymarket/Kalshi use is legal for you
Physical access near a settlement station

title: Scan, Fit, Print — agents that design parts around real objects
thesis: Open-source scanners (a smartphone Orbiter rig, a Raspberry Pi handheld LiDAR, LingBot-Map's video-to-3D) now produce a usable mesh of the thing you need to fit. LLMs already write Blender Python, and they can build a CLI for any app that has no MCP. Point the agent at the scan, have it write parametric CAD that references the scanned surfaces, and you get a custom-fit part on the first print. That is the step generative 3D can't do yet.
why_it_matters: Makers, repair people and small product designers spend most of their CAD time measuring and re-printing. Tolerance-aware agent CAD collapses the loop from 'calipers, sketch, print, fail, repeat' into 'scan, describe, print'. Y-Pan and Gemma Translator show that whole working devices ship as STL plus a bill of materials.
novelty: Every 3D entry in the catalog, from Hunyuan3D and Tripo to text-to-CAD sites, produces visually plausible meshes with no dimensions. The existing natural-language 3D dive is about scenes for screens. Nobody here closes scan, then parametric agent CAD, then a print that fits.

action_sketch: Scan three awkward real objects (a tool handle, a bike mount point, a phone in its case) with the Orbiter workflow or photogrammetry; export clean meshes.

Have Claude Code write a CadQuery/FreeCAD script that imports the mesh, fits planes/cylinders to the contact surfaces, and builds a mount with a stated clearance (e.g. 0.3 mm); prompt it to build its own CLI for the slicer.
Print, test fit, feed caliper measurements back as corrections; log iterations-to-fit for agent vs your hand CAD.
Falsifier: if agent CAD needs more print iterations than your own hand CAD on 3 of 3 objects, the scan-to-parametric step isn't ready — the fitting step, not the scanner, is the bottleneck.

title: Plotted Originals — generative scenes drawn by machine as scarce physical art
thesis: ln turns any 3D scene into hidden-line vector paths, and vpype cuts pen-up travel enough to make long plots practical. LLMs now write the Blender/Python scenes that feed it, and a DuckStation fork rips any PS1 level into OBJ. Pair that with the drawing machines and kinetic sculptures in the art collections and you get a pipeline from AI-generated scene to a one-off ink original. That is a physical answer to the flood of free AI images.
why_it_matters: When images cost nothing, the scarce thing is the physical, signed, slightly imperfect object. Generative artists who move their output onto paper through a plotter, or into motion through a drawing machine, can sell originals through the direct channels the art-market entries describe. Those channels have no gatekeepers.
novelty: The existing generative art dive stays on screens, and the art market dive is about distribution. The pen-plotter entry (S tier) sits in an AI collection, while the drawing machines and kinetic sculptures sit unlabeled in art-i-like. No creator here connects scene generation to machine-drawn editions.

Plot on an AxiDraw or a used plotter (or a DIY GRBL pen plotter) on archival paper; shoot each in window daylight like the print-on-demand guide says.
List 10 numbered originals plus cheaper POD giclée of the same designs; track which sells.
Falsifier: if plotted originals don't sell at a premium over POD prints of the same image after ~20 listings, buyers aren't valuing the physical original and the thesis fails.

title: Ambient Executive Function — glanceable hardware for agents and attention
thesis: OpenAI built a $230 hardware controller for babysitting coding agents. Someone answered with a MacBook-notch status app, and Bot Crossing turned 80 agents into characters who raise their hands. Separately, NFC stickers make logging a habit a one-tap physical act, and Sharp memory LCDs stay on for days at e-paper power. Combine them into a small always-on desk object that shows what needs you, both agents waiting for approval and your own NOW list, and takes physical taps as input. That turns 'out of sight, out of mind' from a willpower problem into an environment.
why_it_matters: For people with ADHD or executive-function friction, the failure is rarely missing information. The information is hidden in a terminal or app they have to remember to open. A glanceable surface with one-tap input removes the remembering step, which is the step that fails.
novelty: The agent-monitor entries treat this as developer convenience, and the habit and self-observation entries treat it as personal productivity. No one in the catalog notices that agent supervision and attention scaffolding are the same interface problem, and that the parts already exist.

Stick NFC tags on desk, water bottle and door: tap = 'done/started/leaving', logged by an iOS Shortcut to the same endpoint; the display updates within seconds.
Run 14 days logging glance-triggered actions (taps within 2 min of a display change) and agent wait time before/after.
Falsifier: if glance-triggered actions fall to near zero by week two (habituation) and agent wait time doesn't drop, ambient display isn't beating a phone notification.

title: Benchmark Your Brain — the skill-optimizer loop, pointed at the human
thesis: The agent world now rewrites skills against benchmarks: SkillOpt rejects any edit that doesn't beat the eval, Karpathy-style autoresearch adds an outer coach loop, and skills log their own failures for batch rewrites. Meanwhile the catalog's learning entries stop at 'turn saves into quizzes'. Run the same loop on yourself. Your saves are the training set, auto-generated quizzes are the eval set, and an outer coach rewrites your study playbook whenever your scores plateau.
why_it_matters: Most people's save folders are graveyards, and this catalog is one. Closing the loop turns passive saving into measured skill gain, and it reports which topics never stick, so you can drop or re-approach them. The same harness already works for agents, so the build is small.
novelty: The existing second-brain and harness dives are about making the AI remember. Nothing in the catalog benchmarks the human. The quiz-generation entry and the SkillOpt entry sit in the same collection without referencing each other.

action_sketch: Export the last 60 days of saves (DejaViewed parquet works) into a table; a weekly Claude skill clusters them into 3 topics and writes 15 retrieval questions each, held out from the study notes.
Quiz yourself cold, log scores per topic; the coach skill rewrites the study playbook (spacing, format: explain-back, build-a-thing, game) only if next week's held-out score beats the last.
Add chat-history mining monthly: questions you re-asked the AI become forced quiz items.
Falsifier: if held-out scores after 6 weeks are no better than a no-coach control topic studied with plain flashcards, the outer loop adds overhead not learning.

title: Offline AI Appliances — one job, one box, no cloud
thesis: Gemma Translator puts speech recognition, translation and TTS on a Raspberry Pi 5, and it ships with a bill of materials and a printable case. Around it, the catalog holds a 100M-parameter local voice cloner, a 3B OCR model that reads 100-page PDFs in one pass, local video search over dashcam footage, 4GB-GPU fine-tuning, and 27B agent models on one 24GB card. Together these are a parts bin for single-purpose AI appliances: a box you hand to someone that does one job, works offline, and never sends their data anywhere.
why_it_matters: The people who most need AI help, like elderly relatives, field workers and privacy-sensitive small businesses, are the least able to manage cloud accounts and the least willing to upload their lives. A purpose-built offline box sidesteps both problems, and a maker with a printer can build it in a weekend.
novelty: Every local-model entry frames the model as something to run on your desktop, and only Gemma Translator ships as an object. Nobody connects the OCR, search, TTS and fine-tune releases into an appliance pattern with an enclosure and a bill of materials.

Falsifier: if latency on the Pi is over ~10s per page or the person reverts to a phone app within a week, the appliance form factor isn't earning its keep at today's edge compute.

title: Mocap as Reward — teaching cheap robots to move like you
thesis: The Microduck RL demo shows the classic failure: a loose reward function makes the robot 'stand' in a way nobody intended. The catalog also holds the fix, scattered across collections. FreeMoCap turns a webcam into markerless motion capture, HY-Motion produces motion from text on robot skeletons, and Blender plus a GPU contact solver can rehearse physical contact. Use captured or generated motion as an imitation reward on a cheap open robot. The reward-design trial and error becomes 'show it what you mean'.
why_it_matters: Hobby robotics is gated by reward engineering more than by hardware. A webcam reference clip gives an individual the motion-prior pipeline that only labs used to have, for small expressive robots, animatronics and installations.
novelty: The robotics entries and the motion and animation entries never reference each other. HY-Motion explicitly supports robot skeletons, yet it's filed as an animation tool. Nobody in the catalog points it at Microduck's reward-hacking problem.

action_sketch: Reproduce the Microduck standing run in its sim with 4,096 envs; confirm the reward hack.
Record a 10-second webcam clip of a 'bob and look around' motion with FreeMoCap (or generate one with HY-Motion), retarget to Microduck's joints, and add a pose-tracking imitation term to the reward.
Compare policies: reward-only vs reward + imitation, scored by a blind viewer on 'looks intentional' and by joint-tracking error; deploy the winner to hardware if you have it.

Falsifier: if retargeting human motion to a duck-scale robot body produces infeasible joint targets that the policy can't track better than the plain reward, the motion prior is the wrong shape for small robots.
